lesson.title: Say Their Names: The Rise of the Black Lives Matter Movement
lesson.summary: Founded in 2013 after George Zimmerman's acquittal, Black Lives Matter grew into one of the largest protest movements in American history following the 2020 killing of George Floyd, drawing on a long lineage of Black activism.
lesson.body:
Black Lives Matter began as a hashtag and a grassroots organizing effort in 2013, founded by three Black organizers, Alicia Garza, Patrisse Cullors, and Opal Tometi, in response to the acquittal of George Zimmerman. Zimmerman, a neighborhood watch volunteer in Sanford, Florida, had fatally shot seventeen year old Trayvon Martin in February 2012, and a jury acquitted him of murder charges in July 2013. The phrase Black Lives Matter, first used by Garza in a social media post, became a rallying cry and then the name of a decentralized network of local chapters and affiliated activists.

The movement grew substantially in 2014, after the deaths of Michael Brown, an unarmed Black teenager killed by a police officer in Ferguson, Missouri in August of that year, and Eric Garner, who died after a New York City police officer placed him in a chokehold during an arrest the same year. Protests in Ferguson drew national and international attention to questions of police use of force, particularly against Black Americans, and to the broader relationship between law enforcement and Black communities. Grand juries in both cases declined to indict the officers involved, which intensified protests and debate.

The movement reached its largest scale by far in the summer of 2020, following the death of George Floyd, a Black man killed by Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin on May 25, 2020. Video of the encounter, in which Chauvin knelt on Floyd's neck for an extended period, circulated widely on social media, and demonstrations spread to cities and towns across the United States and to other countries, becoming among the largest protest movements in American history by some estimates. Chauvin was later convicted of murder in 2021. The 2020 protests also renewed debate over specific policy proposals, including calls in some cities to reduce police department budgets, often summarized as defund the police, a phrase that different activists and organizations defined in different ways, ranging from modest budget reforms to more sweeping calls to reimagine public safety.

Black Lives Matter did not emerge from nowhere. It drew on a long history of Black protest movements in the United States, including the Black Power movement of the 1960s and 1970s, which had itself grown partly out of frustration that the nonviolent tactics of the earlier civil rights movement were not producing fast enough change. Organizations like the Black Panther Party, founded by Huey Newton and Bobby Seale in Oakland in 1966, had emphasized self defense, community programs, and direct confrontation with police practices Black communities viewed as abusive, themes that echo in Black Lives Matter's own critique of policing decades later. At the same time, Black Lives Matter also reflected the organizing tools of its own era: decentralized, social media driven mobilization of the kind that had also powered other grassroots movements of the 2009 to 2020 period, including the ideologically very different Tea Party movement, showing how the same digital organizing tools could serve very different political causes. Public opinion on Black Lives Matter and its policy proposals has been closely divided along political and demographic lines, and Americans continue to debate both the extent of racial bias in policing and the best policy responses to it. What is well documented is the sequence of events, the scale of the 2020 protests, and the movement's roots in earlier eras of Black activism.
